newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italy's Duferco eyeing steel firm Clabecq.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Duferco eyeing steel firm Clabecq.

text.p: Italian-based private steel and commodities trading group Duferco was named on Friday as a candidate interested in taking over bankrupt Belgian steelmaker Forges de Clabecq SA.

Belgium's SWS Walloon regional steel investment arm, which holds a controlling stake in Clabecq, said in a statement Duferco was carrying out a feasibility study into the possibility of taking over all Clabecq's activities.

The possibility of a buyer gives a glimmer of hope to Clabecq's 1,800 workers, who have staged several demonstrations, some violent, in Brussels and at the steel works itself near the town of Tubize about 30 km south of the Belgian capital.
Asked if he were optimistic about contacts with Duferco leading to a takeover, Clabecq's chief executive officer Libert Froidmont was cautious.
"I can't say I'm optimistic, (but) these people are working seriously," he said.
Froidmont said the Italian group had a 1996 turnover of three billion dollars, and that the group so far had not had much presence in central and northern Europe.
Duferco's representatives on Friday met Walloon Region officials and the receivers who have been trying to find a buyer for Clabecq since it went bankrupt in January.
More contacts were due in coming weeks and it was hoped that they would lead to an industrial plan by the end of May.

The SWS said a week ago that three groups had expressed interest in taking over Clabecq and that there was an international firm among them which had been given an exclusive right to negotiate a takeover deal for two months.
The other two were described as Brazilian and a European group.

Clabecq's death sentence was signed in December 1996 when the European Commission rejected a regional aid plan, brandishing it inadmissible state aid for a firm without a future, and the Walloon region pulled the plug on further funding.
Receivers, whose efforts to put together a rescue package failed when the main creditor banks refused to take part, have focused on finding a buyer for the firm as a going concern.
Saddled with high costs, poor margins and low-quality products, Clabecq had struggled to survive in a cyclical industry marked by overcapacity and cheap imports from eastern Europe.

Other Belgian steel firms have shunned the idea of a cooperation or merger with Clabecq, either because they are not interested in its heavy, low grade products or because they have already found another partner.
